summary: This unit teaches you to work with a team on a creative hair, make-up or display project: understand a client's brief, share and research ideas, plan roles, time and budget, give and take feedback, run a trial, and deliver and review the finished work. You will also learn to respect copyright, models' consent and each other's ideas, and to stay safe and hygienic when several people share tools and products.

blocks.p: This unit is about **teamwork in a creative job**. In a salon, a creative job might be the hair and make-up for a wedding party, a Carnival or Independence Day show, a photo shoot, a competition or a window display. One person rarely does it all: a team shares the ideas, the planning and the work. The result is usually better, but only if the team talks, listens and plans.

It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. You will not only learn to make creative looks. You will learn how to agree what the client wants, how to turn ideas into a plan, how to keep to time and budget, how to speak up and listen, and how to learn from the result.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practicals your group plans a themed look from a brief (brief, mood board, design plan and presentation), then creates two matching looks on mannequin heads with a feedback round and a review. The assessor watches how you work with the team as well as the quality of your work.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only boards, sheets, hands and the work on the mannequin heads. Never photograph a person's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **creative brief** is a short written outline of what the client wants. It is the team's starting point and the standard against which the finished work is judged. If the team misunderstands the brief, all the hard work can be wasted.

head: Part of the brief
Question to ask
Example
rows: Theme or idea
What is the look based on?
'Jamaica 62': black, green and gold, for Independence Day.
Audience and place
Who will see it, and where?
A community hall; a church; a photo studio; an outdoor stage in the heat.
Models
How many? Which ages, hair types and skin tones?
Six models: two with natural hair, two relaxed, two wearing braids.
Looks wanted
How many looks, for hair, make-up, accessories?
One hair look and one make-up look for each model.
Colours, mood and style
What feeling does the client want? Anything she does not want?
Bold, joyful, family-friendly; no glitter near the eyes.
Date, time and deadline
When must everything be ready?
Models ready by 6:30 p.m. for a 7:00 p.m. show.
Budget
How much can the team spend, and on what?
J$24,000 for products and accessories.
Who supplies what
Clothes? Accessories? Equipment? Power supply?
The client supplies the garments; the team supplies everything else.

flow: Read the brief together
Underline the key facts
Write a list of questions
Ask the client and write down her answers
Agree one clear summary for the whole team

ul: Read the brief **together**, so that everyone has the same understanding. Several people reading it separately will often understand it differently.
If a part is not clear, **ask the client** before you plan. Do not guess. A short phone call can save days of work.
Write the answers down and share them with the whole team.
A **deadline** is the date and time by which the work must be ready. It cannot move, so the plan is built backwards from it.
Keep the brief where everyone can see it, and check your ideas against it often: does this fit the theme, the budget and the time?

blocks.note: If the client changes the brief later, write the change down, tell the whole team at once and update the plan. Do not rely on one person remembering it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Brainstorming** means the team shares as many ideas as possible in a short time, without judging them. Quantity comes first; choosing comes later.

ol: Agree the aim in one sentence and set a time limit, for example 10 minutes.
One person writes every idea on chart paper or a board, where all can see it.
Everyone adds ideas. Nobody laughs at, argues with or rejects an idea. An odd idea may lead to a good one.
Build on each other's ideas ('and what if we also...').
When the time is up, read the list, group similar ideas and choose the best ones against the brief.

blocks.h: Other ways to organise and find ideas

head: Tool
What it is
Why it helps
rows: Mind map
A drawing with the theme in the centre and branches for related ideas (colours, hairstyles, accessories, music, clothes).
Shows how ideas link, and how many ideas there are around one theme.
Mood board
A collage of pictures, colours, fabrics and textures that shows the look and feeling the team is aiming for.
Everyone can see the same picture. It is quicker than explaining in words.
Research
Looking at photos, films, magazines, nature, fabrics, history and culture linked to the theme.
Gives real examples and fresh ideas; stops you copying one source.
Trends
What is popular now in hair, colour and make-up (from magazines, trade shows and online pages).
A look that feels current suits the audience, but must still fit the brief.
Sketch or face chart
A quick drawing of the hair design, or a printed outline of a face on which make-up colours are planned.
Lets you test and share an idea before using products on a person.

blocks.note: Sources for a look based on a time in Jamaica's history might be old photographs, album covers, films, books, and talking to older family members and clients. Always note where each picture came from, so that you can give credit.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: The basics of colour and texture

blocks.p: Creative looks use colour and texture. A few ideas will help you make choices.

ul: The **colour wheel** is a circle of colours. The three **primary** colours are red, yellow and blue. Mixing two primaries gives a **secondary**: orange, green and violet.
**Complementary** colours sit opposite each other on the wheel (for example blue and orange, or red and green). Side by side they look bright and strong.
**Analogous** colours are neighbours on the wheel (for example yellow, orange and red). Together they look harmonious.
**Warm** colours (red, orange, yellow) feel energetic and close. **Cool** colours (blue, green, violet) feel calm and distant.
Pale versions of a colour (**tints**) and deep ones (**shades**) change the mood. Choose colours that suit each model's skin tone and hair, as well as the theme.
**Texture** is how a surface looks and feels: smooth, rough, shiny, matt, fluffy. A sleek, glossy style looks richer next to a rough or woven accessory. Contrast is interesting; too much looks messy.
Be brief and clear. Say what the idea is and why it fits the brief.
Show it: a sketch, a face chart or a photo is quicker than words.
Listen to questions and to other ideas without interrupting.
Be ready to change or combine your idea with someone else's.

blocks.p: Every member needs a **clear role**, so that nothing is missed and nothing is done twice. Match roles to skills, and share the load fairly, so nobody is overworked or left out. Also give people chances to learn new skills.

head: Role
What she does
rows: Team leader
Keeps the team focused on the brief, the time and the budget; calls meetings; helps settle disagreements; makes the final choice if the team cannot agree; speaks to the client.
Designer or stylist for each look
Plans and carries out a look: sectioning, braiding, colouring, styling, make-up.
Timekeeper
Watches the timeline; warns the team when a step is running late.
Materials and kit person
Keeps the list of products and tools; checks the stock; packs and unpacks; tracks the budget.
Note-taker
Writes the ideas, decisions and actions at each meeting and shares them.
Hygiene and safety checker
Checks that stations are clean, cables safe and products used correctly.

blocks.p: In a small team one person may do several jobs. The jobs still need to be named.

ul: **Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention, looking at her, not interrupting, and checking that you understood ('So you want the braids on the left side?').
Speak clearly and politely. Say what you mean in short sentences.
Invite quieter members by name ('Tamika, what do you think?'). The quiet person may have the best idea.
Agree **one** way to keep in touch, for example a group message or a meeting at the same time each day, and keep to it. Updates scattered across many places get missed.
Write down what is agreed. Short notes, shared with all, avoid arguments later about 'what we said'.

blocks.p: People of different ages, backgrounds and skills see things differently. An older stylist may know classic styles, a younger one may follow new trends, and someone from another parish or culture may know styles, colours and music the others do not. One may be best at braiding, another at colour, another at planning. Together the team produces more ideas and better solutions, and its looks suit a wider range of clients. A good team uses this variety and makes sure nobody is mocked for her background, accent or way of speaking.
Disagreements are normal in a creative team. They become a problem only when they turn personal or when they stop the work.

flow: Stay calm; the leader calls a short, calm meeting
Each person explains her idea and her reasons while the others listen
Go back to the brief: theme, client, models, budget
Test the choices: put them side by side on the mood board or on face charts
Look for a compromise
If still stuck, vote, or the leader or client decides
Write the decision down; thank everyone

ul: **Compromise** means each side gives a little to reach an agreement, for example one person's main colour with the other's accent colour.
Talk about the **idea**, never about the person.
Once the team has decided, everyone follows the decision, even if it was not her first choice. She can raise her concern again at the review.

blocks.note: If you are shy, prepare one point before the meeting and write it down. If you are confident, count to three before you speak, so that others have room.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Feedback** is information about how the work matches the brief and how it could be better. Used well, it improves the work and builds trust. Used badly, it hurts and divides the team.

ul: Choose a good time: soon after the work or the trial, in private or in a team review, never in front of the client or the models.
Talk about the **work**, not the person. Say 'the parting is uneven', not 'you are careless'.
Start with something that works well.
Be **specific**: say exactly what to change and why, so the person knows what to do.
Suggest an idea for improvement. Give one or two points, not a long list.
Check she has understood, and finish on a positive note.

head: Unhelpful
Constructive
rows: 'That is ugly.'
'The colours match the theme well. The lip colour is very strong next to the eye make-up. Could we soften it?'
'Your braiding is bad.'
'The partings are neat. The braids on the left are looser than on the right; try to keep the same tension all through.'
'I do not like your idea.'
'I like the gold. I am worried about the cost. Can we find a cheaper accessory that looks similar?'

ul: Listen without interrupting or arguing, even if you do not agree at first.
Ask questions if something is not clear. Say thank you.
Think about whether the point helps the work match the brief. Use what is useful.
Do not take it as an attack. Taking feedback well shows respect and helps the whole team.

blocks.note: When feedback comes from the client, treat it as the most important feedback of all. Write it down exactly as she says it, and check with her that you have understood.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A good idea fails if it is not ready on time or costs too much. Planning turns the agreed design into a job the team can finish.

flow: List every task
Estimate the time for each task
Decide who does each task
Work backwards from the deadline
Add extra time for delays and travel
Share the timeline with everyone

ul: List all tasks: hair for each model, make-up, accessories, a trial, packing the kit, travel, set-up, touch-ups, clean-up.
Work out how long each look really takes (use the trial). Do not guess.

Remember that stylists work **at the same time**. If each look takes 45 minutes and 4 stylists are working, 4 models can be finished in 45 minutes, and 6 models need two rounds, which is 90 minutes in all.
Start from the deadline and subtract. If everything must be ready by 6:30 p.m. and the work takes 90 minutes, the team must start by 5:00 p.m.
Add a margin for delays (a pin that will not stay, a model who is late). 15 to 30 minutes is common.
Write the **timeline** or **running order**: who does what, and when. Give everyone a copy.
List every product, tool and accessory for every model: combs, clips, pins, hair gel, extensions, colour, brushes, palettes, spatulas, towels, capes, a heat mat, extension cords.
Check stock and who is bringing what. Pack spares (pins, bands, plasters, wipes).
Add hygiene items: disinfectant, tissues, a bin bag, a laundry bag.
A list made before the event means nothing is forgotten on the day.
Add up the cost of everything on the kit list and compare it with the budget in the brief.
If the total is over, find savings that keep the look: cheaper accessories, fewer products, making items yourselves, or sharing tools. If it cannot be done, tell the client and agree a change.
Keep receipts and track what is spent.

head: Item
Cost (J$)
rows: Hair accessories
Hair products
Make-up
Total

blocks.p: If the budget is J$24,000, this list is J$1,300 over. The team must save at least J$1,300 or ask the client.

blocks.note: Always agree any change in cost with the client before you spend the money.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The trial run and doing the work

blocks.p: A **trial run** tests the look on a mannequin head or on a model who agrees, before the real event. There is still time to fix problems.

ul: It shows whether the look matches the brief, suits the model's hair and skin, how long each step really takes, and whether the products and accessories work.
It tests the model's skin for reactions. Follow the maker's instructions for any skin test needed for a colour product.
Take photos from the front, side and back, and write notes.
Afterwards compare the photos with the brief and the mood board. Ask: what worked, what did not, why?
Fix the problems: change the pinning, add a hold product, adjust the timing or add a stylist. Show the client the trial photos and get her feedback. Update the plan and keep a record of the changes.

head: Problem at the trial
Possible cause
Possible fix
rows: Style slips or falls after 30 to 40 minutes
Hair is fine and slippery; too little grip; pins in the wrong place
Add texture or grip product; place pins crossed and close to the scalp; change the method
The look takes much longer than planned
Too many steps; one stylist doing too much
Simplify; share the work; start earlier; add a stylist
Colours look different in photos
Light; skin tone; too much product
Test in the same light as the event; change the shade
Model's skin is red or itchy
Reaction to a product
Rinse off at once; stop using it; record it; see a doctor if it is strong; choose another product

ul: Models have different hair textures, curl patterns, lengths and skin tones. Choose products and methods to suit each one.
Check the models' scalp and skin before you start. Do not work on a model with a cut, a rash or a skin or scalp infection.
Follow the maker's instructions for every product, especially colour. Never mix brands. Do any skin test the maker requires.

blocks.h: Health, safety and hygiene at a show

head: Risk
What the team does
rows: Hot tools
Check cables and plugs; use a heat mat; test for heat before the tool goes near the model; switch off and unplug when not in use; keep cables out of walkways.
Aerosols (hair sprays)
Keep them away from heat and flames; use with good ventilation; tell models to close their eyes.
Shared make-up

Never apply straight from a shared tube or pot. Take a little out with a clean spatula onto a palette. Use a clean brush or disposable applicator for each model. Mascara wands and similar items are single-use, and are thrown away.
Spreading infection
Do not apply make-up near an eye infection or a cold sore. Clean and then disinfect combs and brushes between models. A fresh towel or cape for every model.
Colour products
Gloves; good ventilation; follow the maker's timing; skin test if required.
Spills and clutter
Wipe up at once; keep walkways clear.

blocks.note: Backstage is crowded, hot and fast. This is when accidents happen. One person (the safety checker) should look at cables, spills and hygiene at the start and during the show.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Outdoor shows and shows in halls in Jamaica's heat can make hair styles droop and make-up melt. Test your products in similar heat at the trial, and carry spare pins, blotting paper and water.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Respecting ideas, other people's work and models

ul: Listen to every idea and write it down, even if it is not used.
Give **credit**: when an idea is used, name the person who suggested it and thank her. This is fair and builds trust.
Do not take credit for someone else's work.

blocks.p: **Copyright** is the legal right that protects a person's original photos, drawings, designs and writing from being copied or used without permission. A photo of a hairstyle on a stylist's page belongs to the person who took it.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Using a picture to study and get ideas, for example on a private mood board
This is usually acceptable. Note where it came from.
Copying a look exactly and calling it your own
Do not. Take the ideas and make something new.
Putting someone else's photo on a poster, a website or social media
Ask the owner's permission first, and give credit (name or page).
Showing your own team's work
Use your own photos, taken with the models' agreement.

ul: The model must **agree** before photos are taken and before they are posted. It is best to get her agreement **in writing**.
A model under 18 also needs a parent or guardian to agree.
Explain how and where the photos will be used. If she changes her mind, remove the photos promptly.
If the model or the Centre does not allow faces to be shown, photograph only the hair, hands or work area.
Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act, a person's photo and details are personal information. Keep them private and secure.

blocks.note: When you post a team photo, tag the whole team and give credit to the people who did each part. It tells clients the work is a team effort.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Show the mood board, sketches or face charts, and the trial photos.
Each member explains one part clearly. Say how the design fits the brief, the budget and the time.
Listen to the client's feedback. Write it down. Agree any change, and get her agreement, preferably in writing, before the event.
Keep to the time you have been given.
Hold a short team huddle at the start to confirm the plan and roles.
The leader or timekeeper checks progress against the timeline. If one look is running late, other team members help.
Keep stations clean and safe, and keep the models comfortable.
After the event, clean and then disinfect tools; pack up; launder towels.

blocks.p: Soon after the project, while it is fresh, the team meets for a **review** to learn what went well and what to improve.

flow: Look at the final photos beside the brief and the mood board
Ask: did we match the brief, theme, budget and time?
Collect feedback from the client and the models
Each member says what went well and what could be better
Keep it about the work, not about blaming people
Write a short review sheet with actions for next time
Keep the brief, photos and review sheet in a project file or portfolio

head: Good review question
Why it helps
rows: Did the looks match the brief and the theme?
Tests the result against the client's wishes.
Were we ready on time and on budget?
Shows whether the plan worked.
How well did we communicate and share the work?
Improves teamwork next time.
What will we do differently?
Turns lessons into actions, for example 'do the trial a week earlier' or 'pack spare pins'.

blocks.note: A portfolio of photos and review sheets is also useful for your own career: it shows employers and clients your work and your teamwork.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: I can explain what a creative brief is, what it contains and what to do if it is unclear.
I can use brainstorming, mind maps, mood boards, research and trends to find ideas.
I can explain basic colour and texture words: primary, complementary, warm, cool, tint, texture.
I can show my idea clearly with a sketch, a photo or a face chart.
I can listen actively and include every member of the team.
I can share roles by skills and keep one way to stay in touch.
I can settle a disagreement fairly, using the brief and a compromise.
I can give constructive feedback and receive feedback politely.
I can work back from a deadline, make a timeline and a kit list, and stay within a budget.
I can run a trial, photograph it, compare it with the brief and make changes.
I can work safely and hygienically with hot tools, aerosols, colour and shared make-up.
I can give credit, ask permission to use other people's work, and get models' agreement for photos.
I can present to a client and take her feedback.
I can review a finished project and record what we learned.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'We read the brief together so that everyone has the same understanding of what the client wants.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A short written outline of what the client wants.
The main idea a show or look is based on.
The date and time by which work must be ready.
The amount of money the team may spend.
Sharing many ideas quickly, without judging them.
A drawing that links ideas around one theme.
A collage of pictures, colours and textures showing the look wanted.
A printed outline of a face for planning make-up.
A model head with hair, used to practise styles.
Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel.
How a surface feels or looks: smooth, rough, fluffy.
Giving full attention and checking you understand.
Each side gives a little to reach an agreement.
Specific, kind comments about the work that help it improve.
A plan showing what happens, and when.
A test of the look before the real event.
The legal right that protects original photos and designs from being copied.
Naming the person who made an idea or picture.
The area behind the stage where models get ready.
A talk in which the team shows its finished ideas to the client.
A meeting after the project to learn what went well and what to improve.

c1.title: An Independence Day show in Spanish Town
c1.text: A community group in Spanish Town asks the Centre's team of four trainees to style six models for an Independence Day show. The brief says: black, green and gold; one hair look and one make-up look for each model; models ready by 6:30 p.m. for a 7:00 p.m. show; a budget of J$24,000. The team's list is hair accessories J$9,500, hair products J$8,000 and make-up J$7,800. Each hair look takes 45 minutes, and the make-up is done during the styling. All four trainees can work at the same time.

c2.title: A disagreement over colour at the Centre
c2.text: The team is planning a portfolio photo shoot at the Centre. Tashane wants gold as the main colour, and Marlon wants deep green. Their voices rise and the rest of the team go quiet. The team leader, Petra, knows the brief asks for a 'rich, natural look for a graduation photo' and that the models' skin tones range from light to very dark.

c3.title: A poster, a photo and a young model
c3.text: Trainee Shanelle finds a photo of an updo on a professional stylist's online page and wants it as the main picture on the team's poster for a show. The team also took photos of Jodian, a 17-year-old model, at the trial. Jodian agreed to be photographed, and the team would like to post the photos on the Centre's social media page.

c4.title: A trial run in Mandeville
c4.text: At the trial, Kerry's braided crown on Abigail, who has very fine, silky hair, slips after 40 minutes. It took 65 minutes to do, though the plan allowed 40. Abigail's scalp near the nape is red and itchy where a temporary colour gel was used.

c5.title: Backstage at a fashion show
c5.text: Backstage at a show in Montego Bay, eight models are getting ready. One lipstick tube is being passed from model to model. A flat iron lies on a table, and its cable runs across the walkway where stylists carry cans of hairspray. Chenelle, one of the models, has a cold sore at the corner of her lip.

questions.q: By how much is the team's list over the client's budget?
questions.why: The three items add up to J$9,500 + J$8,000 + J$7,800 = J$25,300. The budget is J$24,000, so the list is J$1,300 over.

questions.q: Which change best brings the list within budget and keeps the brief's look?
o: Make fabric flowers in the theme colours instead of buying accessories
Spend the extra J$1,300 and tell the client after the show is over
Use cheaper products on the models whose styles will be most visible
Leave out the green and use only black and gold, which cost a little less
questions.why: A saving must keep the theme. Making simple accessories in the right colours saves money without losing the look. Dropping a colour breaks the brief, and spending more without asking is not agreed.

questions.q: What is the latest time the team can start styling, if every model must be finished by 6:30 p.m.?
questions.why: Four stylists work at once, so four looks take 45 minutes and the other two need a second round: 90 minutes in all. 6:30 p.m. minus 90 minutes is 5:00 p.m.

questions.q: What should Petra do first?
o: Vote at once, so that the argument ends as quickly as possible
Call a short, calm meeting and ask each to give her reasons
Ask the other members to say whose idea they like the least
Choose gold, because Tashane has been in the team for longer
questions.why: A leader keeps the argument from becoming personal, then lets each person explain while the others listen. Hurrying to a vote or favouring one person solves nothing and hurts trust.

questions.q: Which method is the fairest way to choose between gold and green?
o: Use both colours in equal amounts, even if the look turns out muddy
Test both on face charts and the mood board against the brief
Ask the client to pick without showing her either option
Let the person who speaks the loudest choose, since she feels strongest
questions.why: The brief is the standard. Putting both choices side by side and checking them against the theme, the models' skin tones and the budget gives a fair, factual answer, and a compromise may emerge.

questions.q: Marlon is asked to comment on Tashane's work. Which comment is the most constructive?
o: It is fine, but you need to work faster than you are doing now
Your work is messy and I do not think it will look good in photos
Everyone knows gold is overdone; green would have been better
The gold on the cheek is lovely; blend its edge to look softer
questions.why: Constructive feedback names something that works, is specific about what to change and why, and is about the work, not the person.

questions.q: Which use of the stylist's photo does not need her permission?
o: Keeping it on a private mood board, with a note of its source
Printing it on the poster as the main picture, with no name beside it
Posting it on the Centre's page and saying the team created it
Copying the look exactly and showing the result as an original idea
questions.why: Looking at a picture for ideas, with the source noted, is fine. Printing or posting it publicly needs permission and credit, and presenting a copy as original is dishonest.

questions.q: What is needed before the team posts Jodian's photos?
o: The agreement of the team leader, who was present at the trial
Only the agreement of the Centre, as it owns all the photos
Her agreement and a parent's or guardian's, ideally in writing
Her own agreement alone, since she was happy to be photographed
questions.why: A model under 18 needs a parent or guardian to agree as well, and written agreement is best. Taking a photo is not the same as agreeing to its use online.

questions.q: A week after the photos go up, Jodian asks the team to take them down. What should they do?
o: Ask her to wait until the show is over
Leave them up, since she signed the form a week ago
Replace them with a photo that shows only one side of her face
Remove them promptly and tell her it is done
questions.why: A model who changes her mind has the right to have the photos removed. Act promptly and confirm to her that it is done.

questions.q: What is the most useful first step for the slipping braided crown on very fine hair?
o: Find the cause, then add grip and pin crossed near the scalp
Pull the braids much tighter so that they cannot move at all
Use the same method on the show day and hope for better results
Use a hairspray with a much stronger hold and a stronger smell
questions.why: Fine, silky hair is slippery. Finding the cause and changing the method, such as adding texture or grip and pinning better, fixes the problem; tight pulling hurts the model and may cause traction damage.

questions.q: The look took 65 minutes, but the plan allowed 40. What is the best way to plan the show day?
o: Cut the make-up and accessories without asking the client first
Ask some of the models to arrive later so that fewer are done
Update the timeline to 65 minutes, add a stylist or start earlier
Keep the 40-minute plan and make up the time by rushing the last steps
questions.why: The trial exists to show the real time. Use it to rebuild the timeline, start earlier or share the work, rather than rushing, which spoils the look and the safety.

questions.q: What should the team do about Abigail's red, itchy scalp?
o: Carry on, as itching is a normal sign that the colour is working
Rinse the gel off at once, record it and choose another product
Leave the gel on for a little longer to see whether the colour takes
Cover the red area with a thick layer of her usual hair cream
questions.why: Redness and itching may be a reaction. Remove the product, do not use it on her again, record it, and advise a doctor if it is strong. Her comfort and safety come before the look.

questions.q: What should the team do with the trial photos?
o: Compare them with the brief, then show them to the client
Delete the photos that show problems, so that no one sees them
Keep them private, since trial photos are not useful later on
Post them online at once to see what other people think of them
questions.why: Trial photos show what works and what does not. Comparing them with the brief, then showing the client, lets the team and client agree changes in good time.

questions.q: How should the lipstick be used for the eight models?
o: Used straight from the tube on each model, as long as she does not mind
Rubbed on with the stylist's finger so that the colour goes on evenly
Taken out with a clean spatula, then applied with a clean brush
Wiped with a tissue after each model, then used straight from the tube
questions.why: A shared tube touching many mouths spreads germs. Taking a little onto a palette with a clean spatula and using a clean brush for each model prevents that.

questions.q: What should the team do about Chenelle's cold sore?
o: Ask her to leave the backstage area, so that she does not infect the other models
Tell the leader and use only disposable applicators away from the sore
Cover the sore with concealer taken from the team's shared palette
Apply lipstick over it so that her lips look the same as the others
questions.why: A cold sore is infectious and painful, and shared products can spread it. Avoid it, use disposable applicators and tell the leader. Covering it with shared products spreads the infection, and there is no need to humiliate her.

questions.q: What should be done about the flat iron and its cable?
o: Leave it switched on, but put a warning sign beside the cable
Tape the cable flat to the floor and leave the iron where it is
Move the iron a little further away from the hairspray cans
Switch it off, unplug it and clear the cable from the walkway
questions.why: A loose cable is a trip hazard and a hot tool left on is a burn and fire risk, especially near aerosols. Switch off, unplug, rest it on a heat mat and keep cables out of walkways.

questions.q: Why must hairspray cans be kept away from the flat iron?
o: The heat makes the spray lose its hold before it reaches the hair
The smell of the spray may make the iron switch itself off
The spray is flammable and the can may burst if it is heated
The spray leaves a film on the plates that makes the iron rust
questions.why: Aerosols hold flammable gas under pressure. Near heat they can catch fire or burst. Store them away from hot tools and use them with good ventilation.

questions.q: Which colour is complementary to blue on the colour wheel?
o: Yellow
Orange
Green
Violet
questions.why: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel. Opposite blue is orange. Green and violet are its neighbours (analogous) and look harmonious with it.

questions.q: The team has a braider, a colour specialist, a make-up artist and a planner. Which sharing of roles is best?
o: Give all the jobs to the most experienced person and let the others watch
Let each person choose any job, even if she has never done it
Give the planner every job, as she will see the full picture
Match each person to her best skill, and share the extra jobs fairly
questions.why: Matching roles to skills gets better work, and sharing the load fairly stops one person from being overloaded. Everyone also needs the chance to learn.

questions.q: A model has a sleek, glossy ponytail. Which accessory adds the most contrast of texture?
o: A rough woven raffia wrap
A polished, shiny metal band
A glossy plastic hair clip
A smooth, shiny satin ribbon
questions.why: Texture contrast comes from putting different surfaces side by side. A rough woven wrap stands out against smooth, glossy hair, whereas smooth satin, plastic and metal are all smooth and shiny like the hair.
